summary: This document specifies the Authentication-Results message header field for email. It records the results of message authentication checks so that mail filters and Mail User Agents can relay the information or use it to sort and filter. It was later replaced by RFC 7601.

eli5.summary: Email gets a stamp saying which sender checks passed or failed, so mail programs can sort accordingly. A newer version replaced this.

questions: what does dkim=pass mean in email headers
how do mail servers record spf and dkim results
subtitle: A standard email header that records which sender checks a message passed, so later software can sort and filter on them.

tldr.problem: Email servers run checks such as DKIM and SPF on incoming messages, but mail filters and mail programs downstream had no common place to read the results.
tldr.mechanism: A trusted server adds an Authentication-Results header field naming itself, then listing each check as method=result with optional reasons and the message properties that were examined.
tldr.outcome: The header is only as trustworthy as the server that added it, so servers must delete forged copies at the edge of their domain. RFC 7001 has since been obsoleted by RFC 7601.

today: RFC 7001 is a Proposed Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 7601, which is now the place to look for the current definition. It was also updated by RFC 7410, and it replaced RFC 5451 and RFC 6577.

sections.title: Why a Results Header Exists
sections.content:
RFC 7001 defines the Authentication-Results header field for email. It collects, in a machine-readable form, the results of message authentication work so that a Mail User Agent (MUA) or a downstream filter can make filtering decisions or give the user a recommendation about where the message really came from.

It revises the original definition in RFC 5451 and folds in errata. The methods it covers include DKIM, SPF, SMTP AUTH, ADSP, VBR and a new reverse-IP check called iprev, plus the older DomainKeys and Sender ID. The goal is a common framework so that each new scheme does not need its own header field.

The RFC does not say what to do with the results. How a filter acts on them or how an MUA shows them is local policy and user interface design. It also places no requirement on servers to reject messages that fail checks.
sections.eli5: Instead of every mailbox inventing its own sticker for 'this was checked', everyone uses the same sticker, in the same place, with the same words.

sections.title: Format of the Header Field
sections.content:
The field is a structured trace field. Its value is an authserv-id naming the checking service, an optional version, and then one or more statements of the form method=result. Each statement can carry a reason string and ptype.property=value items that show what was examined, such as smtp.mailfrom (the SMTP MAIL FROM value). If no checks were done, the field can say none.

The ptype is one of smtp, header, body or policy. The policy type records that a local policy changed or overrode a result. For example, an ADMD might turn a DKIM pass into a failure because the Subject field was not signed.

The authserv-id must be unique to the administrative domain that generated it, and consumers use it to decide whether to trust or ignore a field. Common practice is to use the domain's DNS name; a hostname also works but is harder to manage at scale. An optional version token, where this specification is version 1, lets a parser stop when it meets a version it does not know.
sections.eli5: The stamp says who stamped it, then lists each check and whether it passed, like a report card with the subject name and the grade next to each other.

sections.title: Methods and Result Values
sections.content:
Each method returns a result from a defined set. DKIM and DomainKeys share one set: none, pass, fail, policy, neutral, temperror and permerror. SPF adds softfail, and its meanings come from the SPF specification. The policy result means the check itself succeeded but local policy found the outcome unacceptable, for instance a passing SPF result for a domain on a local list of unacceptable domains.

SMTP AUTH is reported as auth with results none, pass, fail, temperror and permerror. Consumers SHOULD treat fail and temperror as the same thing here, since the client did not authenticate in either case.

Other methods registered elsewhere are vbr, dkim-atps and dkim-adsp. New methods and result codes MUST be registered with IANA. Experimental ones are only for domains that agreed to use them, and production software SHOULD ignore or delete fields that contain them.
sections.eli5: Each check gives one of a few grades such as pass, fail or 'could not check right now'. A grade of 'policy' means the check passed but the house rules still say no.

sections.title: The iprev Reverse Lookup Check
sections.content:
This RFC defines one new method, iprev. The checker takes the connecting client's IP address, looks up the names for it (a PTR query), then looks up the addresses of each of those names (A and AAAA queries). The test succeeds if the original address appears among those addresses.

Implementations MUST limit how many names they follow so as not to burden DNS; the RFC cites SPF's limit of 10 as an example. There is no none result, because every email connection has an IP address.

The RFC is cautious about the method. It notes that forward and reverse DNS often do not match in some regions, so the exact way a verifier runs the test is left open. It also points to guidance that applications should avoid using this test for authentication or security, and says that including it is an acknowledgement that the method is common, not an endorsement.
sections.eli5: It is like calling back the phone number a caller gave you to see whether the same person answers. It is a rough check, and the RFC warns not to lean on it too hard.

sections.title: Adding and Removing the Header
sections.content:
A compliant server that runs authentication checks adds the field, either once per check or once covering all results. It MUST NOT add a result to an existing field. The field is prepended, above other trace fields the server adds, so a consumer can tell which copies sit inside the trusted part of the path and which came from outside.

The central safety rule is in Section 5. Because the field has no protection of its own, any server MUST delete any instance that claims, by its authserv-id, to have been added inside its trust boundary but did not come from a trusted server. A border server could instead remove all instances on incoming mail, or keep those from a list of trusted external checkers.

Consumers are told to be wary. MUAs and filters SHOULD NOT interpret the field unless configured to, and SHOULD only act when the authserv-id matches one used in their own domain. They MUST ignore results with unregistered result codes or ptypes and results for methods they do not support. MUAs SHOULD NOT show results to users without careful human-factors design, since an attacker could register a look-alike domain, sign mail and still get a pass.

If local policy is to reject on a hard failure, the border server SHOULD refuse the message during the SMTP exchange instead of adding the header, which avoids generating bounce messages known as backscatter.
sections.eli5: The mail room must scrape off any stamps that arrive from outside pretending to be its own, and the people inside should only trust stamps with their own mail room's name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The main danger is forgery. A malicious sender can add a field using a victim domain's name as the authserv-id and claim the message was authenticated. A non-conformant server will not strip it, and a trusting MUA may believe it. For that reason, processing should be off by default and enabled only after the border server is verified as compliant, and any list of trusted hostnames should start empty.

The RFC lists alternative protections that have not been developed for lack of demand, such as signing the field with DKIM, or carrying the results as message metadata through an SMTP extension and an IMAP counterpart.

A second danger is false confidence. A pass does not make a message trustworthy: spam can be signed with DKIM by the spammer or a compromised system and still pass. The RFC also covers misuse of the iprev check for denial of service, backscatter, attacks on the authentication methods and compromised internal hosts.
sections.eli5: A stamp saying 'checked and fine' only helps if nobody can fake the stamp. And even a real stamp does not mean the letter is nice, only that it was checked.

viz.caption: DKIM AND DOMAINKEYS RESULT VALUES (RFC 7001 SECTION 2.6.1)

items.label: Verified
items.desc: Signed, acceptable to the domain, and verification passed.

items.label: Verification failed
items.desc: Signed and acceptable, but verification failed.

items.label: Unacceptable signature
items.desc: Signed, but some aspect was not acceptable to the domain.

items.label: Unprocessable
items.desc: Signed, but with syntax errors or otherwise not processable.

items.label: Transient error
items.desc: Likely temporary problem; a later attempt may succeed.

items.label: Permanent error
items.desc: Unrecoverable problem; a later attempt is unlikely to help.
